papers.title_in_file: Quantum vs. Classical Machine Learning: A Benchmark Study for Financial Prediction
papers.version_note: arXiv:2601.03802v1 [cs.LG], 7 Jan 2026. The text layer is the single preprint copy. Tables are partly jumbled in the layer; numbers taken from tables are named in reader_inference and anchors, and values keep to what the quotes hold.
papers.what_it_is: A benchmark of QNN, QLSTM and QSVR models against architecture-matched classical models on directional prediction, live trading and realized-volatility forecasting for U.S. and Turkish equities, all run in noiseless simulation.

existing.note: Value is right. Anchor correction: the 7-D S&P 500 passage is Section IV-B (page 15) and the conclusion sentence is in Section V (page 18), not V-B p.16 and p.19. The result is one final walk-forward fold (fold 5) on one index.
existing.value: The authors report that the classical ANNs performed slightly better than the QNNs, with higher AUC and accuracy, and conclude that classical models retain an advantage on mid-range cross-asset features.
existing.anchor: Section IV-B part b (7-D feature set), p.15; Table X, p.15; Section V Conclusion, p.18

classical models retain an advantage on mid-range cross-asset features
existing.reader_inference: Table X puts the ANN at accuracy 0.7289 and AUC 0.7657 against 0.7221 and 0.7498 for the Hybrid-SQ QNN: gaps under one point of accuracy and under two points of AUC, from a single run and a single fold, with no interval reported. The QNN has higher recall in the same table.

existing.note: The underperformance is one regime only: F4 (Post-pandemic, 2022-2024). The two gain regimes are F1 (2008-09) and F2 (2018-19). In F3 the QLSTM Sharpe is lower but the Sortino ratio is slightly higher. Anchor correction: Section IV-C, page 16 (table on page 17), not V-C p.17.
existing.value: The authors report that, in a live trading simulation across four distinct market regimes of the S&P 500, the QLSTM improves risk-adjusted returns in two of four regimes (the Global Financial Crisis, 2008–09, and the Pre-COVID phase, 2018–19), and that in the Post-pandemic regime the QLSTM underperforms economically against the LSTM (ARC −15.15%, Sharpe −0.694 against ARC 35.16%, Sharpe 1.523).
existing.anchor: Section IV-C, F4 bullet and Key Observations, p.16; Table XII, p.17
quotes: we assessed both LSTM and QLSTM models in a live trading simulation across four distinct market regimes of the S&P 500.
QLSTM improves riskadjusted returns in two of four market regimes, namely the Global Financial Crisis (2008–09) and the Pre-COVID phase (2018–19), despite only modest AUC gains.
F4 (Post-pandemic): QLSTM underperforms economically (ARC −15.15%, Sharpe −0.694) versus LSTM (ARC 35.16%, Sharpe 1.523).
existing.reader_inference: With one run per regime, no confidence interval and no significance test on the trading results, two wins and two losses in four regimes does not separate the QLSTM from the LSTM. Test AUCs in Table XII lie between about 0.507 and 0.545.

existing.note: The gains are for the final walk-forward fold only (test 2020-01-02 to 2021-12-31). Also, KCHOL is a Turkish stock in the 3-D feature set (Table IX), while AAPL is in the 64-D set (Table XI): the paper's Key Observations call both gains 'higher-dimensional'. Section IV-B and Tables IX and XI, pages 14 to 16.
existing.value: The authors report that hybrid quantum neural networks surpass the parameter-matched ANN by +3.8 AUC and +3.4 accuracy points on AAPL stock and by +4.9 AUC and +3.6 accuracy points on Turkish stock KCHOL, on the final walk-forward fold (testing period 2020-01-02 to 2021-12-31).
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section III-C2, p.8; Tables IX and XI
quotes: In directional classification, hybrid quantum neural networks surpass the parameter-matched ANN by +3.8 AUC and +3.4 accuracy points on AAPL stock and by +4.9 AUC and +3.6 accuracy points on Turkish stock KCHOL.
We report results for the final fold, which has a training period from 2009-01-07 to 2019-12-31 and a testing period from 2020-01-02 to 2021-12-31.
existing.reader_inference: Table IX (3-D set) gives KCHOL ANN AUC 0.7475 and QNN AUC 0.7968 (difference 4.9 points) and accuracy 0.6747 against 0.7106 (3.6 points). Table XI gives AAPL AUC 0.597 against 0.635 and accuracy 0.5720 against 0.606. So the KCHOL gain is from the low-dimensional regime, which conflicts with the Key Observations label. In the same tables the ANN is ahead on 4 of 5 Turkish tickers and, from the jumbled Table XI pairing, on BA and DVN.

existing.value: The authors state that all quantum models are executed in simulation using statevector simulation with exact expectation values.
quotes: All quantum models are executed in simulation mode.
Quantum circuits are evaluated using statevector simulation with exact expectation values.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own setup statement in Section IV-A, p.15.
existing.reader_inference: No hardware run and no noise model is reported anywhere in the paper, so every quantum result is noiseless and shot-noise free, although Section IV-D invokes shot noise when it discusses amplitude encoding.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study compares QML models with architecture-matched classical counterparts across three financial tasks: directional return prediction on U.S. and Turkish equities, live-trading simulation with Quantum LSTMs versus classical LSTMs on the S&P 500, and realized volatility forecasting using Quantum Support Vector Regression.
quotes: we present a reproducible benchmarking framework that systematically compares QML models with architecture-matched classical counterparts across three financial tasks
(ii) live-trading simulation with Quantum LSTMs versus classical LSTMs on the S&P 500, and (iii) realized volatility forecasting using Quantum Support Vector Regression.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of its scope (abstract, p.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that QNNs are evaluated against ANNs for directional classification, QLSTMs against LSTMs for live trading, and QSVRs against kernel SVRs for volatility forecasting.
quotes: Specifically, QNNs are evaluated against ANNs for Directional Classification, QLSTMs against LSTMs for live trading, and QSVRs against kernel SVRs for volatility forecasting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own scope statement, Section III-A, p.5.
assertions.reader_inference: Section III-E also adds GARCH(1,1) as a volatility baseline, and Table II lists GARCH among the models compared.

assertions.value: The authors state that daily prices are retrieved via the Yahoo Finance API, that adjusted close is used for individual equities and the close price for the S&P 500, and that any day with missing observations is removed so that all tickers share a common trading calendar.
quotes: Daily prices for each of the tickers (in both the markets) are retrieved via the Yahoo Finance API1.
For individual equities, we use adjusted close which accounts for stock splits and dividends. For the S&P 500 benchmark, we use the close price directly.
we remove any day with missing observations, retaining only dates with complete data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own data setup, Section III-B, p.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the U.S. universe combines the S&P 500 benchmark with five representative firms spanning different capitalizations and sectors, and that a parallel Turkish universe is constructed to mirror this sectoral diversity.
assertions.anchor: Section III-B, p.5; Tables III and IV
quotes: The U.S. universe combines the S&P 500 benchmark with five representative firms spanning different capitalizations and sectors (Table III).
A parallel Turkish universe is constructed to mirror this sectoral diversity
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own scope, Section III-B, p.5.
assertions.reader_inference: The universe is ten single stocks plus one index. The Turkish set has no index benchmark, and the volatility study uses only four of the assets (S&P 500, AAPL, KCHOL, GARAN).

assertions.value: The paper defines the directional target as binary: the label is one when the closing price exceeds the previous closing price and zero otherwise, and each day is labeled up or down by that rule.
assertions.anchor: Section II-A1 (Eq. 1), p.3; Section III-C, p.6
quotes: directional models cast forecasting as a binary decision: will today’s closing price exceed yesterday’s?
Each day is labeled as “up” or “down” according to the binary rule in Eq. 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition given in Eq. 1 and Section III-C.

assertions.value: The authors define a 3-dimensional feature set (d = 3) for the Turkish equities, built from adjusted-close prices as three momentum indicators: RSI-14, the raw stochastic oscillator %K-14, and a 3-day simple moving average of %K14.
quotes: we define a 3-dimensional feature set containing three input variables (d = 3).
(1) RSI-14 The 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI-14) measures the magnitude of recent gains versus losses on a 0– 100 scale
a 3-day simple moving average of %K14 smooths out noise and confirms true momentum shifts.
assertions.certainty_reason: Feature definition, Section III-C1a, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors define a 7-dimensional feature set (d = 7) for the S&P 500 made of same-day log-returns of five non-U.S. indices and two U.S. proxies (DJI, NYA), with the U.S. proxies lagged by one day.
assertions.anchor: Section III-C1b, p.7; Table V caption
quotes: the 7-dimensional feature set which contains seven input variables (d = 7)
Our feature set, therefore, consists of same-day log-returns of five non-U.S. indices and two U.S. proxies (DJI, NYA).
U.S. proxies are lagged by one day (we use DJIt−1 and NYAt−1 when predicting day-t S&P 500).
assertions.certainty_reason: Feature definition, Section III-C1b, p.7.
assertions.reader_inference: Fig. 3(B) labels all seven inputs 'Lag 1', while the text says same-day returns for the five non-U.S. indices. The two statements differ on timing.

assertions.value: The authors define a 64-dimensional feature set (d = 64) for U.S. equities: seven days of returns from eight global indices (56 features) together with the stock's own past eight daily returns.
quotes: we summarize the 64-dimensional feature set (d = 64) used for U.S. equities (Table III).
we construct a lag-matrix embedding that includes seven days of returns from eight global indices (56 features) together with the stock’s own past eight daily returns.
assertions.certainty_reason: Feature definition, Section III-C1c, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors state that the directional features are scaled to the range [0, 1] by min-max normalization fitted on the training fold, with a five-fold walk-forward expanding-window scheme, and that results are reported for the final fold.
quotes: the raw input features are scaled to the range [0, 1] using min-max normalization.
The min-max scaler is fitted on the training fold and applied to the corresponding test fold to prevent look-ahead bias.
we adopt a walk-forward, expanding-window crossvalidation scheme with five folds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own evaluation setup, Section III-C2.
assertions.reader_inference: Only fold 5 is reported in the results tables, although the text says QNNs are competitive 'across folds'; folds 1 to 4 are not shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that min-max scaling is not applied where feature-specific constraints make it unnecessary, giving the low-dimensional Turkish ANN baseline as the example.
quotes: Exceptions arise where feature-specific constraints, such as bounded momentum indicators, make scaling unnecessary (e.g., the lowdimensional Turkish ANN baseline).
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup statement, Section III-C2, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: The 3-D comparison therefore gives the ANN and the QNN different input preprocessing, which the paper does not say it tested for effect.

assertions.value: The authors state that four QNN variants are explored (QNN-SQ, QNN-MQ, Hybrid-SQ, Hybrid-MQ), along two axes: a classical preprocessing layer or none, and single-qubit or multi-qubit readout, with a grid search over circuit depth L from one to six.
quotes: This yields four architectural variants:
For each QNN variant, we conduct a grid search over the depth of the quantum layer (L ∈ {1, . . . , 6}) and
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own model-search setup, Section III-C3a.
assertions.reader_inference: Several selected QNNs sit at the grid edge of six layers (KCHOL, AAPL, LNC in Tables IX and XI), so the best depth may lie outside the searched range.

assertions.value: The authors state that angle encoding is used for the 3-D and 7-D feature sets with one qubit per feature (3 and 7 qubits), and that amplitude encoding, which embeds 2 to the power n features into n qubits (printed flat as 2n in the text layer), is used for the 64-D set, with n treated as a hyperparameter over 2 to 6.
quotes: For the 3-D and 7-D feature sets, we employ angle encoding, where each feature requires a dedicated qubit. This results in 3 and 7 qubits, respectively
we use amplitude encoding, which embeds 2n features into n qubits, reducing the requirement to n = 6 qubits for 64 features.
we treat n ∈ {2, . . . , 6} as a hyperparameter in the grid search for the 64-D case
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own encoding setup, Section III-C3a, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: With n below 6, a 64-feature vector cannot fit in the qubits; the paper does not say how features are reduced for n of 2 to 5 (the Hybrid variants add a classical projection).

assertions.value: The authors report the chosen ANN baselines as shallow networks: [3-11-1] with 56 parameters for 3-D, [7-32-16-1] with 801 parameters for 7-D, and [64-32-1] with 2,113 parameters for 64-D, picked by validation AUC after a grid search over hidden-layer widths.
quotes: Low-dimensional (3-D): [3–11–1] with one hidden layer of 11 neurons, totaling 56 parameters.
Medium-dimensional (7-D): [7–32–16–1] with two hidden layers (32 and 16 neurons), totaling 801 parameters.
High-dimensional (64-D): [64–32–1] with one hidden layer of 32 neurons, totaling 2,113 parameters.
select the optimal ANN based on validation AUC.
assertions.certainty_reason: Counts follow from the stated layer sizes; the grid itself is not shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The counts check out as weights plus biases: 3x11+11+11+1=56; 7x32+32+32x16+16+16+1=801; 64x32+32+32+1=2,113.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QNN and ANN parameter counts are comparable, in ranges of about 40 to 60 (low), 100 to 1000 (medium) and 2000 to 2200 (high).
quotes: This ensures QNNs and ANNs have comparable parameter counts: ∼40–60 (low), ∼100–1000 (medium), and ∼2000–2200 (high).
assertions.reader_inference: No table gives the parameter count of the selected QNNs. The medium range spans a factor of ten, so 'parameter-matched' is only loosely supported by what is printed.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for both QNN and ANN families, candidate models are trained on expanding windows and compared by mean AUC across five validation folds, the highest mean AUC wins, and ties go to the model with fewer parameters.
quotes: candidate models are trained on expanding windows and evaluated via mean AUC across five validation folds. The architecture with the highest mean AUC is selected; if multiple architectures achieve the same AUC, the one with fewer parameters is chosen.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own selection protocol, Section III-C3c, p.8.
assertions.reader_inference: Selection uses the mean over all five validation folds, and fold 5 is also the reported test fold. The reported fold therefore took part in choosing the architecture, which can bias both arms upward. The QNN grid (four variants, depth 1 to 6, qubit counts) is larger than the ANN grid (hidden widths), so any such bias may favor the QNN more.

assertions.value: The paper defines AUC as a measure of the model's ability to rank positive instances higher than negative ones across all classification thresholds, and states that it is threshold-agnostic and robust to class imbalance.
quotes: AUC assesses the model’s ability to rank positive instances higher than negative ones across all classification thresholds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition in Section III-C4, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors report that, on the 3-D feature set, QNNs show competitive performance to ANNs; the ANNs often achieve higher accuracy and AUC, QNNs match or exceed them in certain cases, especially recall, and the best-performing QNNs use deeper layers and multi-qubit readout.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-B part a, p.15; Table IX, p.14
quotes: Our analysis on the low-dimensional 3-D feature set reveals that across folds, QNNs demonstrate competitive performance to ANNs.
While ANNs often achieve higher accuracy and AUC, QNNs are able to match or exceed them in certain cases, especially in the context of recall.
the best-performing QNNs on this feature set are architectures with deeper layers and Multi-Qubit Readout strategy employed.
assertions.reader_inference: In Table IX the ANN has higher accuracy and AUC on GARAN, TCELL, TUPRS and ULKER, and the QNN is ahead on KCHOL. QNN recall is higher on KCHOL and TUPRS only; on TCELL it is 0.3858 against 0.6693. 'Especially recall' is therefore not uniform. The Conclusion's phrase 'Shallow QNNs perform well on compact features' sits against 'deeper layers' here (depths 3 to 6).

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 7-D S&P 500 feature set the QNN posts a better recall than the ANN, and that the Hybrid-SQ architecture with shallow depth and single-qubit readout is the best performing architecture.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-B part b, p.15; Table X caption
quotes: The performance comparison results for directional classification on 7-D feature set are presented in Table X We observe that, for the medium-dimensional experiment on S&P 500
Similar to the case of low-dimensional (3-D) feature set, QNNs model posts a better recall.
The Hybrid-SQ architecture with shallow depth and single-qubit readout is the best performing architecture on this feature set.
the Hybrid-SQ QNN (depth 3, Hybrid=True, MQR=False) shows competitive performance, trading off marginal accuracy for improved recall.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 64-D feature set QNNs remain competitive with ANNs, attain a higher AUC than the ANN on AAPL with accompanying accuracy gains, and are only marginally worse on the rest of the tickers; Table XI's caption adds that the Hybrid-MQ QNN achieves a large recall gain on DVN and that ANNs retain the edge on accuracy and AUC for other tickers.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-B part c, p.15; Table XI caption, p.16
quotes: The performance comparison results for directional classification on 64-D feature set are presented in Table XI.

In this regime, QNNs remain competitive with classical ANNs. They attain a higher AUC than the ANN on AAPL with concomitant gains in accuracy. On the rest of the tickers, their performance is only marginally worse.
ANNs, however, retain the edge on accuracy and AUC for other tickers.
assertions.reader_inference: Table XI's text layer pairs the BA row as ANN accuracy 0.677 and AUC 0.738 against QNN 0.5930 and 0.6180, and the DVN row as AUC 0.6750 against 0.6080. If that pairing is right, the gaps on BA (about 12 AUC points) and DVN (about 7) are not 'marginal'. The table is jumbled in the text layer, so the pairing is inferred.

assertions.value: The authors state that hybrid QNNs yield their strongest improvements in higher-dimensional feature spaces, outperforming parameter-matched ANNs on AAPL and on KCHOL, while achieving comparable accuracy on the remaining assets.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-B part d, Key Observations, pp.15-16
quotes: ture spaces, outperforming parameter-matched ANNs on AAPL (+3.8 AUC / +3.4 pp accuracy) and KCHOL (+4.9 AUC / +3.6 pp accuracy), while achieving comparable accuracy on the remaining assets.
assertions.reader_inference: KCHOL belongs to the 3-D regime (Table IX), so 'higher-dimensional' fits only AAPL. The 'comparable accuracy' wording does not match the BA gap read from Table XI (see res-64d-us).

assertions.value: The authors state that circuit depth, hybrid preprocessing and readout design are the main determinants of QNN effectiveness, and that hybrid preprocessing lets shallower circuits stay competitive with ANNs while multi-qubit readout helps deeper architectures.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-B part d, Key Observations, p.15
quotes: Circuit depth, hybrid preprocessing, and readout design are the main determinants of QNN effectiveness.
Hybrid preprocessing enables shallower circuits to remain competitive with ANNs while multi-qubit readout enhances deeper architectures
assertions.reader_inference: The paper shows only the best architecture per ticker; it gives no ablation that varies one factor with the others fixed, so the 'main determinants' wording is not tested by a reported experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that live trading is evaluated on the S&P 500 from 2008 to 2024, split into four regimes: the Global Financial Crisis (2008–2009), the Pre-Covid era (2018–2019), the Covid Shock & Recovery (2020–2021) and the Post-pandemic era (2022–2024).
quotes: We evaluate live trading on the S&P 500 from 2008–2024 which we segment into four representative regimes:
(i) the Global Financial Crisis (2008–2009) (ii) the Pre-Covid era (2018–2019), (iii) the Covid Shock & Recovery (2020–2021) and (iv) the Post-pandemic era (2022–2024).
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own regime definitions, Section III-D1, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors report that t-tests find no significant difference in mean returns between the compared regimes (all p-values greater than 0.05), that variance tests show highly significant differences (p-values below 0.001), and that Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests confirm the return distribution shapes differ.
quotes: The t-tests indicate that average returns do not significantly differ between regimes (all p-values are greater than 0.05).
the variance tests show highly significant differences in return volatility across all comparisons with p-values below 0.001.
the KS test results confirm that the overall shape of return distributions changes meaningfully.
assertions.reader_inference: Table VII covers three pairs only (F1 vs F3, F1 vs F2, F2 vs F4). The regimes are separated by variance and shape, not by mean. The paper cites Welch (1947) as the reference for the KS test.

assertions.value: The authors state that the live-trading features are the previous-day log return, the MACD line (difference of the 12-day and 26-day exponential moving averages), the MACD signal (a 9-day EMA of the MACD line) and the 14-day RSI, stacked in rolling windows of length T = 10 trading days, so each input sample is a 10 by 4 matrix.
quotes: the MACD line, defined as the difference between the 12day and 26-day exponential moving averages (EMAs) [65]
the MACD signal, a 9-day EMA of the MACD line
the RSI14, a 14-day Relative Strength Index
We stack these features into rolling windows of length T = 10 trading days. Each input sample is thus a matrix xt ∈ R10×4
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own feature setup, Section III-D2, p.10.

assertions.value: The authors state that their QLSTM follows the design of an earlier quantum LSTM in which each classical gate of a standard LSTM cell is replaced with a variational quantum circuit, varying qubit width q over 3, 4 and 5 and circuit depth L over 2 to 6.
quotes: Our QLSTM design builds on the architecture proposed by [59], where each classical gate in a standard LSTM cell is replaced with a variational quantum circuit (VQC).
(i) Qubit width (q ∈ 3, 4, 5), which sets the embedding dimension for each gate, and (ii) Circuit depth (L ∈ 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own model definition, Section III-D3a.

assertions.value: The authors state that the LSTM baselines use hidden sizes 3, 4 and 5 with 2 to 6 stacked layers, that the resulting parameter counts match the QLSTM family, and that this ensures differences reflect quantum versus classical computation rather than raw size.
quotes: we construct LSTM models with hidden state sizes h ∈ 3, 4, 5 and stacked layers L ∈ 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
The resulting parameter counts match the QLSTM family, which ensures that differences reflect quantum versus classical computation rather than raw size.
assertions.reader_inference: Table XII lists the selected models, and their sizes differ: fold 3 has an LSTM of 1426 parameters against a QLSTM of 386, and fold 2 has 325 against 476. Matched families do not give matched selected models.

assertions.value: The authors state that model probabilities become position signals in {-1, 0, +1} by two thresholds (long above tau-long, short below tau-short, otherwise no trade), and that a 0.05% transaction fee is applied whenever the position changes.
quotes: This probability is converted into a position signal st ∈ {−1, 0, +1}.
A 0.05% transaction fee is applied whenever the position changes, ensuring profitability is evaluated net of trading costs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own backtest setup, Section III-D4, p.11.

assertions.value: The authors state that the generated signals are compared against a simple buy-and-hold strategy that goes long the S&P 500 at the start of each fold and holds throughout.
quotes: As a benchmark, we compare the generated signals from both QLSTM and LSTM against a simple buyand-hold strategy.
an investor goes long st = +1 on the S&P 500 at the start of each fold and holds the position throughout the entire period.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own benchmark statement, Section III-D4.
assertions.reader_inference: No buy-and-hold result appears in Table XII or in the text of Section IV-C, so the stated benchmark comparison is not reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that each regime fold is split 70/10/10/10 for training, early stopping, model selection and threshold calibration, that early stopping uses AUC with a patience of 30 epochs, and that the threshold pair maximizing Sharpe is selected for the final backtest.
quotes: Each of the four market regime folds is split in the ratio 70/10/10/10 (see Fig. 8) for training, early stopping, model selection, and threshold calibration phases.
fails to improve for a fixed patience window (30 epochs).
The pair that maximizes Sharpe is selected for final backtesting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own validation setup, Section III-D5.
assertions.reader_inference: The four slices add to 100% of each regime, and the text does not name the dates on which the reported test metrics are computed (Fig. 8 only labels an arrow 'Test on hold-out period'). The paper also says model configurations are picked by highest AUC on the 10% model-selection slice and later that final models maximize Sharpe on the tau slice; the two statements differ.

assertions.value: The paper defines the live-trading metrics as annualized return (the geometric average yearly return), annualized standard deviation, the Sharpe ratio (excess return per unit of total risk) and the Sortino ratio (a downside-focused analogue of Sharpe that penalizes only negative volatility).
quotes: ric average yearly return. Let rt be the per-period
Sortino Ratio: A downside-focused analogue of Sharpe that penalizes only negative volatility.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definitions in Section III-D6.
assertions.reader_inference: The numeric risk-free rate used for Sharpe and Sortino is not stated. Table XII's caption lists maximum drawdown, but the table has no such column.

assertions.value: The authors state that both live-trading models are trained against the labels with a weighted binary cross-entropy loss to account for class imbalance in the directional labels.
quotes: a weighted BCE loss Lwbce to account for the class imbalance in directional labels.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own training setup, Section III-D3c.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the Global Financial Crisis regime (F1) the QLSTM improves risk-adjusted returns over the LSTM despite similar AUC (0.5446 against 0.5334).
assertions.anchor: Section IV-C, F1 bullet, p.16; Table XII, p.17
quotes: F1 (Global Financial Crisis): QLSTM improves risk-adjusted returns over LSTM despite similar performance on AUC (0.5446 vs. 0.5334).
assertions.reader_inference: Table XII gives F1 ARC of -0.0167 (LSTM) and 0.0596 (QLSTM) and Sharpe of -0.0477 and 0.3865. The text sentence on annualized return ('-1.67% to +5.96%') is garbled.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the Pre-Covid regime (F2) the QLSTM lifts ARC from 7.45% to 11.03% and reduces ASD by about 40% (0.150 to 0.088), giving a Sharpe ratio of 1.26 against 0.50.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-C, F2 bullet, p.16; Table XII, p.17
quotes: F2 (Pre-Covid): QLSTM lifts ARC from 7.45% to 11.03% and reduces ASD by ∼ 40% (0.150 → 0.088), yielding a Sharpe ratio of 1.26 versus 0.50.
assertions.reader_inference: The selected QLSTM here has 476 parameters against 325 for the LSTM (Table XII).

assertions.value: The authors report that in the Covid regime (F3) the QLSTM AUC is higher (+0.011) but Sharpe is lower (0.766 against 0.895) as ASD rises (0.235 to 0.262), while the Sortino ratio is slightly higher for the QLSTM.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-C, F3 bullet, pp.16-17; Table XII
quotes: F3 (Covid shock & recovery): QLSTM’s AUC is again higher (+0.011), but Sharpe is lower (0.766 vs. 0.895) as ASD rises (0.235 → 0.262). The Sortino ratio is slightly higher for QLSTM

assertions.value: The authors state that the F4 shortfall is return-driven rather than risk-driven (ASD 0.231 for the LSTM against 0.218 for the QLSTM) and indicates that the fixed threshold calibration learned on the tau-slice does not transfer well to this regime for the QLSTM, even though its AUC ranking is slightly better.
quotes: ASD is marginally lower for QLSTM (0.231 → 0.218), so the shortfall is return-driven rather than risk-driven.
This indicates that the fixed threshold calibration learned on the τ -slice does not transfer well to this regime for QLSTM, even though its ranking (AUC) is slightly better.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment re-calibrates the thresholds to test this explanation.

assertions.value: The authors state that live-trading performance is highly sensitive to threshold selection and that Sharpe-maximizing long/short cutoffs significantly influence realized returns.
quotes: Performance is highly sensitive to threshold selection; Sharpe-maximizing long/short cutoffs significantly influence realized returns.
assertions.reader_inference: No table varies the thresholds. The statement is a reading of the F4 result, not a reported sensitivity run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the improved Sharpe ratios in F1 and F2 suggest the QLSTM's score calibration aligns closely with return magnitudes under volatile conditions.
quotes: The improved Sharpe ratios during these periods suggest QLSTM’s score calibration aligns closely with return magnitudes under volatile conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that classifier skill is modest for both models in live trading, but that trading outcomes differed markedly once scores were thresholded into positions.
quotes: Although the classifier skill is modest across both regimes for both of the models, the trading outcomes differed markedly once scores were thresholded into positions
assertions.reader_inference: Table XII shows test AUC between about 0.507 and 0.545, close to the 0.5 of a random ranking.

assertions.value: The authors state that the volatility target is the 5-day rolling realized variance, predicted one step ahead, and that forecasts are evaluated on two U.S. assets (the S&P 500 index and Apple Inc.) and two Turkish assets (Koc Holding and Turkiye Garanti Bankasi).
quotes: Our prediction target is the 5-day rolling realized
We evaluate forecasts on two U.S. assets (S&P 500 index, Apple Inc.) and two Turkish assets
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup, Section III-E, p.12.

assertions.value: The authors state that the volatility features combine the past p returns and the past q realized variances, trained with an expanding window from an initial 720 days and retrained every 120 days, with total training window lengths of 1000, 2000, 3000 and 4000 days also examined for robustness.
quotes: Our feature set is composed of the past p values of returns and past q values of realized variance
We begin with an initial training set of 720 days, and every 120 days, the model is retrained using all available past data to account for potential regime shifts.
we also experiment with total training window lengths L ∈ {1000, 2000, 3000, 4000} days.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own setup, Section III-E1.
assertions.reader_inference: The values of p and q, the out-of-sample dates and the results for the four window lengths are not given in the text. Fig. 2 names a rolling 1000-day split for this study, while the text describes an expanding window.

assertions.value: The paper defines GARCH(1,1) as a model in which conditional variance is a linear function of the previous day's squared shock and the previous day's variance estimate, with a constant term greater than zero and non-negative shock and persistence coefficients, and requires a stationarity condition so that volatility does not diverge.
quotes: By including GARCH(1,1) alongside SVR and QSVR, we establish our benchmarking against a standard econometric baseline.
ω > 0 is a constant term, α ≥ 0 captures the immediate impact of new shocks, and β ≥ 0 reflects the persistence of volatility over time.
To ensure that volatility does not diverge, the model requires a stationarity condition:
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition in Section III-E2a.

assertions.value: The paper defines the quantum kernel as the squared magnitude of the overlap between feature-mapped states, with the SVR solving its dual quadratic program on a pre-computed kernel matrix, and states that kernel evaluation scales as O of N squared (printed flat as O(N 2)) in the number of samples N.
quotes: the SVR solves its dual quadratic program using the pre-computed kernel matrix, where the optimization depends only on inner products
Kernel evaluation scales by O(N 2) where N is the number of samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition and cost statement in Section III-E2c.

assertions.value: The authors state that the angle-encoded map uses hardware-efficient RY-RZ rotations with a ring of CZ entanglers repeated L times, that the amplitude-encoded map embeds the normalized feature vector in the amplitudes of ceil(log2 d) qubits followed by a fixed randomly sampled unitary layer stack, and that an exponent beta in {1, 2, 3} is introduced on the overlap (printed flat as 2 beta in the exponent).
assertions.anchor: Section III-E2c, p.13; Eq. 17 to 19; Fig. 9
quotes: where each unitary block Urot consists of a hardware-efficient RY –RZ rotations with a ring of CZ entanglers. This is repeated L times (depth).
we introduce an exponent β ∈ {1, 2, 3}
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the feature maps, Section III-E2c.

assertions.value: The authors state that in simulation the kernel entries are deterministic because they are built from exact statevector overlaps, and that on real quantum hardware such overlaps would need to be estimated through measurement-based fidelity tests.
quotes: In simulation, kernel entries are deterministic since they are built from exact statevector overlaps.
On real quantum hardware, by contrast, such overlaps would need to be estimated through measurement-based fidelity tests (e.g., SWAP or Hadamard).
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own scope statement, Fig. 9 caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that rigorous proofs of quantum advantage remain an open problem.
quotes: Although rigorous proofs of quantum advantage remain an open problem
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of a limit, Section III-E2c.

assertions.value: The authors state that hyperparameters for every SVR and QSVR variant are tuned with Optuna (Bayesian optimization with Tree-structured Parzen Estimators), and that for the QSVR the exponent beta, a second parameter alpha and the entanglement topology are also hyperparameters.
assertions.anchor: Section III-E3, p.14; Table VIII caption
quotes: Optuna is a Bayesian optimization library that efficiently explores high-dimensional search spaces through techniques such as Tree-structured Parzen Estimators (TPE).
For our QSVR, α, β, and the entanglement topology are also hyperparameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own tuning setup, Section III-E3 and Table VIII.
assertions.reader_inference: The QSVR has more tuned dimensions (qubits, layers, alpha, beta, topology) than the RBF SVR (C, epsilon, gamma). The number of Optuna trials is not stated.

assertions.value: The paper defines QLIKE as a volatility-specific loss in which forecasts that are too low are punished more heavily than forecasts that are too high, with lower scores better, and states that Diebold-Mariano tests are used to decide whether QSVRs forecast better than their classical counterparts.
quotes: Forecasts that are too low get punished more heavily than forecasts that are too high.
we also carry out Diebold–Mariano Test to determine whether QSVRs provide better forecasts than
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition in Section III-E4.
assertions.reader_inference: Table XIII and XIV report only DM p-values (QSVR as reference); the DM statistics and their signs are not shown, although the text cites 'positive DM statistics'.

assertions.value: The authors report that QSVRs with angle embedding consistently outperform linear and polynomial SVRs on QLIKE (positive DM statistics) across all four tickers, though they still lag the RBF kernel.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-D part a, p.17; Table XIII
quotes: Table XIII shows that QSVRs with angle embedding consistently outperform linear and polynomial SVRs on QLIKE (positive DM statistics) across all four tickers, though they still lag the RBF kernel.
assertions.reader_inference: In Table XIII the KCHOL QLIKE is -6.4352 for the QSVR and -6.4247 for the RBF SVR, so on KCHOL the QSVR does not lag the RBF kernel (the DM p-value against RBF is 0.095). The GARAN polynomial QLIKE prints as a positive 60.5361, presumably a lost sign.

assertions.value: The authors state that an angle-encoded QSVR attains the lowest QLIKE on KCHOL and remains within about 0.02 to 0.04 QLIKE of the best classical kernels on S&P 500 and AAPL.
quotes: an angle-encoded QSVR attains the lowest QLIKE on KCHOL and remains within ∼0.02–0.04 QLIKE of the best classical kernels on S&P 500 and AAPL.
assertions.reader_inference: Table XIII differences are 0.034 (S&P 500, -8.2937 against -8.3277) and 0.021 (AAPL, -7.3888 against -7.4101). On KCHOL the margin over RBF is about 0.01 and not significant at 5% (p = 0.095).

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the angle-encoded QSVR, DirAcc remains stable around 0.60, often on par with or slightly below the best classical models.
quotes: Importantly, DirAcc remains stable around 0.60, often on par with or slightly below the best classical models.
assertions.reader_inference: In Table XIII the QSVR DirAcc is below the RBF SVR on all four tickers (for example 0.6287 against 0.6467 on AAPL). The later Key Observation that QSVRs 'frequently match or slightly exceed classical models' holds against linear, polynomial and GARCH, not against RBF.

assertions.value: The authors report that with amplitude encoding at d = 32 the QSVR attains competitive QLIKE, that increasing to d = 64 results in clear degradation, and that the QSVR delivers its best performance at d = 32.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-D part b, p.17; Table XIV; Key Observation, p.18
quotes: With d = 32, the model attains competitive QLIKE performance, but increasing dimensionality to d = 64 results in clear degradation
QSVR delivers best performance when d = 32.
assertions.reader_inference: Only d = 32 (5 qubits) is tabulated (Table XIV). In that table the QSVM QLIKE is worse than linear and polynomial SVR on GARAN (-5.6154 against -6.0734) and KCHOL (-6.1804 against -6.2909), and worse than the RBF SVR on all four tickers. The d = 16 and d = 64 results have no table.

assertions.value: The authors state that the degradation at the higher dimension is expected because amplitude encoding requires precise state preparation and numerical instability compounds as the embedding dimension grows, and that practical implementations must balance d against circuit depth and shot noise.
quotes: This sensitivity is expected because amplitude encoding requires precise state preparation, and numerical instability compounds as the embedding dimension grows.
practical implementations must carefully balance d against circuit depth and shot noise.
assertions.reader_inference: All runs use exact statevector simulation without shot noise, so neither numerical instability nor shot noise is measured by a reported experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that QLIKE values consistently position QSVRs between RBF SVRs (best) and linear/polynomial SVRs (worst), and that R2 values show moderate explanatory power for QSVRs compared with the RBF SVRs, which still dominate in absolute fit.
quotes: QLIKE values consistently position QSVRs between RBF SVRs (best) and linear/polynomial SVRs (worst).
R2 values show that QSVRs offer moderate explanatory power in comparison to classical RBF SVRs which still dominate in absolute fit.
assertions.reader_inference: Table XIV (amplitude) contradicts 'consistently': QSVM QLIKE lies below linear and polynomial SVR on GARAN and KCHOL. Table XIII has the QSVR ahead of RBF on KCHOL, and in Table XIII GARCH has the best MSE and R2 on the S&P 500 (R2 0.5106 against 0.4734 for the RBF), so 'RBF dominates in absolute fit' does not hold on that asset.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that quantum models can compete with or surpass classical approaches in certain settings: shallow QNNs perform well on compact features, amplitude encoding enables useful signal extraction from higher-dimensional data, QLSTMs improve risk-adjusted returns in multiple regimes, and QSVRs reliably match or exceed linear SVRs, while classical models retain an advantage on mid-range cross-asset features.
quotes: Our results show that quantum models can compete with or surpass classical approaches in certain settings.

Shallow QNNs perform well on compact features, amplitude encoding enables useful signal extraction from higher-dimensional data, QLSTMs improve risk-adjusted returns in multiple regimes, and QSVRs reliably match or exceed linear SVRs.
assertions.reader_inference: Four statements in this sentence do not match tabulated results: 'shallow' (best 3-D QNNs are deeper, depth 3 to 6), 'amplitude encoding ... useful' (64-D ANN leads on BA and DVN), 'multiple regimes' (two of four), and 'reliably match or exceed linear SVRs' (Table XIV, GARAN and KCHOL).

assertions.value: The authors describe their work as a reproducible benchmarking framework that standardizes data splits, features and evaluation metrics, and state that random seeds are fixed at both NumPy and PyTorch levels to guarantee deterministic runs across folds.
quotes: we present a reproducible benchmarking framework
Random seeds are fixed at both NumPy and PyTorch levels to guarantee deterministic runs across folds.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no code or data repository link, and does not state p and q, the number of Optuna trials or the volatility test dates. A single fixed seed means no variation across seeds is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that applying angle encoding to the 64-D feature set would require 64 qubits, which they call impractical in the NISQ era.
quotes: applying angle encoding to the 64-D feature set would require 64 qubits, which is impractical in the NISQ era.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of a limit, Section III-C3a.

assertions.value: The authors state that a straightforward QLSTM implementation of the classical benchmark of Fischer and Krauss would require millions of circuit executions, far beyond the capacity of current noisy quantum hardware.
quotes: A straightforward QLSTM [59] implementation of the same experiment would require millions of circuit executions which is far beyond the capacity of current noisy quantum hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no count or derivation for 'millions of circuit executions'.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Support Vector Regression remains largely unexplored for realized-volatility forecasting, with prior studies mostly examining generic regression or classification tasks.
quotes: Quantum Support Vector Regression (QSVR) remains largely unexplored for realized-volatility forecasting.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that properly tuned classical ML models typically achieve 55-65% directional accuracy.
quotes: properly tuned classical ML models typically achieve 55–65% directional accuracy [51], [52]

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that LSTMs trained on large datasets such as Chinese market returns or S&P 500 constituents achieve statistically significant improvements in directional accuracy.
quotes: LSTMs trained on large datasets, such as Chinese market returns [48] or S&P 500 constituents [11], achieve statistically significant improvements in directional accuracy

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that quantum recurrent architectures trained on only self-lag returns collapse into trivial persistence models unless they incorporate sufficient exogenous features.
quotes: quantum recurrent architectures trained on only self-lag returns collapse into trivial persistence models unless they incorporate sufficient exogenous features [40]

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Leung, Daouk and Chen (2000), that predicting the direction of index returns often produces more consistent trading performance than forecasting return values.
quotes: Leung, Daouk, and Chen (2000) [41] show that predicting the direction of index returns often produces more consistent trading performance than forecasting return values.
